Article Title: Trump signs order to ease diesel costs, ‘save millions of dollars’ for farmers
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump

Diesel still costs well above last year

Trump drops diesel export ban

US President Donald Trump on Monday (local time) signed an executive order aimed to ease the burden of high diesel prices on farmers, truckers and other businesses, as fuel costs continue to put pressure on Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections.Trump announced the move during a campaign stop in Grand Island, Nebraska, saying that loosening limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel would save farmers “millions” and help bring down the cost of goods and groceries.“Pete and Jim, this should absolutely ensure your election, I guarantee you that,” Trump said, addressing Republican governor Pete Ricketts and governor Jim Pillen.The order directs states to increase the availability of tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is used in farming, construction and other industries. It also calls on states to consider waiving certain fuel taxes and includes so-called non-enforcement of dyed diesel limitations.Red-dyed diesel is exempt from federal and state excise taxes. The administration says that temporarily easing restrictions would reduce costs for businesses that depend on diesel.“The typical trucker will save more than $100 every time they fill up,” Trump said as he signed the order before a crowd in Grand Island.“Farmers will also save millions and millions of dollars, and this order will also drive down the cost of all goods and to go to grocery prices very substantially.”The steps also include the treasury department reviewing certain taxes on diesel.Ten states accounting for roughly a third of US diesel sales had already taken steps to allow wider use of dyed diesel by Friday, according to research firm ClearView Energy Partners, cited by Politico. Several states had also waived taxes on diesel used in agricultural vehicles.The move comes as diesel prices remain sharply higher than a year ago.The average price of diesel fell to $6.32 a gallon on Monday, down 13 cents from the previous week but still $2.63 higher than a year ago, according to AAA.Fuel prices have surged amid the ongoing war against Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. The conflicts have contributed to a significant decline in the amount of diesel available on the global market.Exports of American diesel have also risen to record levels since the US and Israel launched a war with Iran in February and Ukraine began targeting Russian refineries.The red-dyed diesel measure follows weeks of uncertainty over how the administration would respond to rising fuel prices.Trump had repeatedly backed an outright ban on diesel exports as agriculture-state Republicans, including Iowa Senator Chuck Grassley, pushed for action to lower costs for farmers.Energy secretary Chris Wright and White House energy advisers had been working on alternatives.But on Friday, Trump ruled out a diesel export ban and said he had never really considered one, after Europe agreed to release fuel from its diesel reserves.Agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins said Monday morning that Trump would announce additional short-term relief for farmers in Nebraska and that she would also discuss the issue during a stop in Iowa.High fuel and grocery prices have become a major concern for rural voters, many of whom have backed Trump and Republicans in recent elections. Nebraska farmers and ranchers have also been angered by the administration's plan to allow more imports of foreign beef.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed to ease the burden of high diesel prices on farmers, truckers and other businesses. The order directs states to increase the availability of tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is used in farming, construction and other industries. It also calls on states to consider waiving certain fuel taxes.

Article Title: Karnataka OKs auto approval of period leave for govt staff
Article Text:
Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar

App-authorised leave can’t be reversed





BENGALURU: Women govt employees across Karnataka will no longer need to justify their need for menstrual leave with their sanctioning authority, as the state govt Monday ordered automatic approval of all such leave applications through the Kartyavya app.In a move aimed at ensuring menstrual leave remains an entitlement rather than a matter of discretion, the latest directive from the Praja Seva department has made the leave-sanctioning process virtually automatic, eliminating the need for human intervention. Officials have been instructed to ensure that employees apply for menstrual leave only through the Kartyavya app.The Kartyavya app is an AI-powered mobile attendance registration platform. Once a menstrual leave application is authorised through the app, no sanctioning authority can withhold, question or reverse the decision.The decision follows recent reports that women employees were facing hurdles in availing the leave, with applications allegedly being held up and some sanctioning officers even questioning the need for such leave.The state govt has now made it clear that such discretion cannot be exercised once the prescribed conditions are met. The circular issued by Praja Seva department said state govt had already extended a day’s menstrual leave every month to women govt employees. The benefit was specifically introduced to do away with the need for a medical certificate.“An application that fulfils the prescribed conditions should be sanctioned promptly, and the sanctioning authority has no discretion to reject it,” the circular further clarified.
Article Summary: Women govt employees across Karnataka will no longer need to justify their need for menstrual leave with their sanctioning authority. The state govt Monday ordered automatic approval of all such leave applications through the Kartyavya app. The decision follows recent reports that women employees were facing hurdles in availing the leave.

Article Title: Lucknow floods: 60 boats deployed, more on way, UP govt steps up relief
Article Text:
District administration has intensified flood relief operations as Gomti River levels rise in Lucknow





LUCKNOW: The district administration has intensified flood relief operations in low-lying areas as rising Gomti River levels continue to inundate several localities, prompting deployment of additional boats, distribution of relief kits and tighter security in affected neighbourhoods.District magistrate Vishakh G said nine gram panchayats in Bakshi Ka Talab tehsil remain waterlogged. Within the Lucknow Municipal Corporation limits, Faizullaganj and nearby settlements such as Mama Colony, Lauramau and Daud Nagar are among the worst hit, with water entering residential lanes and disrupting movement.Relief kits supplied by the Uttar Pradesh relief commissioner’s office are being distributed to affected families. Officials said each kit contains 10 kg wheat flour, 10 kg rice, 10 kg potatoes, along with chana, pulses, bottled drinking water and other essential items.To maintain connectivity and speed up relief delivery, the administration has deployed 60 boats in Faizullaganj. Vishakh G said more than 20 motorised boats from Ayodhya and other districts are expected to arrive by Tuesday, which is likely to expand evacuation capability and allow residents to commute for basic needs.Security has been stepped up in submerged localities, with SDRF boats assisting local police in patrolling flooded stretches and monitoring locked homes. The district magistrate said one person was recently arrested for allegedly attempting to steal from abandoned houses in an inundated area.Calling the situation challenging, Vishakh G appealed for public cooperation and urged residents to follow official advisories.Meanwhile, executive engineer Mukesh Kumar Vaish of the irrigation department’s Gomti river division reported that the water level at Gau Ghat was 108.45 metres on Monday evening, while the Central Water Commission’s Hanuman Setu gauge recorded 107 metres and the Gomti Barrage level was about 106.75 metres.Vaish said differences in readings occur due to the river’s natural gradient, with slopes of around 10–15 cm per km leading to variations between gauge points. At Hanuman Setu, the danger mark is 109.5 metres and the highest flood level is 110.85 metres, according to the CWC.
Article Summary: District administration has intensified flood relief operations as Gomti River levels rise in Lucknow. Nine gram panchayats in Bakshi Ka Talab tehsil remain waterlogged. More than 20 motorised boats from Ayodhya and other districts are expected to arrive by Tuesday.

Article Title: ‘Learn Hindi or leave job’: Bengaluru Zomato warehouse manager booked for threatening Kannada-speaking staff
Article Text:
A shift manager named Ashok Muttayy was accused of telling Kannada-speaking workers to learn Hindi





BENGALURU: A 31-year-old shift manager at a Zomato-rented warehouse near Nelamangala was booked for allegedly telling Kannada-speaking workers to learn Hindi or leave their jobs.Ashok Muttayy, who hails from Andhra Pradesh, worked as a shift manager at the warehouse in Madanayakanahalli.According to police, a video surfaced on social media showing Ashok speaking to workers in Hindi during an official interaction. When a worker asked him to speak in Kannada, Ashok allegedly refused and told the workers to learn Hindi or leave their jobs.Soon after, a group of pro-Kannada activists gathered outside the warehouse and demanded action against Ashok.“We registered a suo motu case and filed a petition against Ashok for his act. Ashok later apologised for his conduct,” an investigating officer told TOI.
Article Summary: Ashok Muttayy, 31, was booked for allegedly telling Kannada-speaking workers to learn Hindi or leave their jobs. A video surfaced on social media showing Ashok speaking to workers in Hindi during an official interaction. Pro-Kannada activists gathered outside the warehouse and demanded action against Ashok.

Article Title: CJP assault case: Swatantra Bhardwaj gets regular bail after 3-week interim relief
Article Text:
Bhardwaj had earlier been granted three weeks' interim bail with strict conditions.

Why was Bhardwaj arrested?

(With agency inputs)





NEW DELHI: A Delhi court on Tuesday granted regular bail to social media influencer Swatantra Bhardwaj in connection with the alleged assault on the father of a student activist during a protest at Jantar Mantar.Bhardwaj had earlier been granted three weeks' interim bail with strict conditions. The court has now granted him regular bail after considering his conduct during the interim bail period.A detailed order, including the bail conditions, is expected to be passed later in the day, according to news agency ANI.On September 15, the court had granted Bhardwaj three weeks' interim bail and said his conduct during the period would be considered before deciding his regular bail plea.It had barred him from posting, publishing or discussing the case, his defence or the complainant's family on social media or any media platform.He was also restrained from contacting the complainant, his daughter or any witness and from tampering with evidence.The court had observed that “bail is an expression of the court’s trust, and it is not a trophy to be displayed”, while cautioning against public celebrations following release on bail.Bhardwaj was detained in Bulandshahr on September 4, hours after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protested outside the Parliament Street police station demanding his arrest over the alleged assault.The action followed outrage over an interview in which Bhardwaj claimed that he had “cracked the skull” of the student activist's father during the June 23 protest and that he escaped arrest because of his 'political connections'.Police, however, had disputed the severity of the injuries claimed by Bhardwaj, saying the man suffered a simple head injury during a scuffle.Bhardwaj was subsequently remanded to judicial custody on September 7 and lodged in Tihar Jail. He was released from the prison on September 18 after being granted interim bail.
Article Summary: Bhardwaj had earlier been granted three weeks' interim bail with strict conditions. The court has now granted him regular bail after considering his conduct during the interim bail period. A detailed order, including the bail conditions, is expected to be passed later in the day.

Article Title: Pilot who 'never planned to fly': Mumbaikar Smit Machchhar's journey from textile course to saving 180 lives on flydubai flight
Article Text:
Captain Smit Machchhar managed to regain control of a flydubai aircraft after a co-pilot attacked him

From textile engineering to cockpit

From SpiceJet to flydubai

The flight that plunged thousands of feet





MUMBAI: Captain Smit Machchhar never grew up dreaming of flying planes. In fact, when he was 19, his career path appeared to be taking him in an entirely different direction — towards his family's textile business.An aviation seminar during a management course changed that.More than a decade later, the Mumbaikar found himself at the controls of a flydubai Boeing 737 MAX during one of the most terrifying moments of his flying career — after his co-pilot allegedly attacked him in the cockpit as the aircraft was carrying 174 passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv.Despite being injured, Machchhar is reported to have fought back and helped prevent the aircraft from plunging further. The plane had dropped thousands of feet in a matter of seconds before passengers and crew intervened and the aircraft was eventually diverted to Saudi Arabia.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later identified Machchhar as the captain and praised his actions, saying he had helped prevent a major disaster.Machchhar's journey into aviation was anything but conventional.In a podcast interview recorded around a year before the incident, he recalled that becoming a pilot was not a childhood ambition.After school, he initially enrolled in a textile engineering course because he expected to eventually contribute to his family's business.He later opted for a management course to prepare himself for the business.It was during that course, when he was just 19, that he attended an aviation seminar."Unlike a lot of other aviators right now, aviation was not like a childhood dream," Machchhar said in the interview.The seminar changed his plans.His decision to enter aviation initially worried his mother."My mom was scared," he recalled, explaining that commercial aviation was far less familiar to people around him 15-17 years ago. His father, however, was more comfortable with his decision.Machchhar subsequently completed his commercial pilot training in New Zealand before obtaining his Boeing 737 type rating at the Flight Safety Training Centre (FSTC) in Manesar, Gurgaon.Machchhar joined SpiceJet in 2011 and spent more than a decade with the airline, eventually becoming a senior commander and Line Training Captain.According to his professional profile, he accumulated more than 9,500 flying hours with SpiceJet, including over 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command. As a Line Training Captain, he was responsible for training, assessing and mentoring other pilots while ensuring adherence to operational and safety procedures.He moved to flydubai in June 2022 as a direct-entry captain and has since been flying the Boeing 737 fleet.His profile lists more than 9,750 hours of flying experience and experience on the Boeing 737-800 and Boeing 737 MAX 8/9.A senior pilot who had trained Machchhar previously described him as a "very decent and sober person" who was always willing to learn.Machchhar's brother is also a pilot with flydubai.The flydubai flight was carrying 174 passengers, including 166 Israeli citizens, when the incident unfolded.According to flight-tracking data, the Boeing 737 MAX descended from roughly 30,875 feet to 16,750 feet in just 29 seconds. Flightradar24 recorded an extreme descent rate of around 30,000 feet per minute.Reports said the Omani co-pilot attacked Machchhar with a knife. The captain was injured but managed to resist while the aircraft was in danger of losing control.Passengers and crew eventually entered the cockpit and subdued the attacker.The aircraft was then diverted and landed at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia. Two additional pilots who had been travelling as passengers were also on board and later took over the aircraft.The severity of the descent surprised aviation experts. Former United Airlines pilot and aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said he was surprised the aircraft remained intact after the extreme manoeuvre, while aviation investigator Jeff Guzzetti said the aircraft had enough altitude left for the pilots to recover.The aircraft also reportedly suffered damage to its rudder during the descent.
Article Summary: Captain Smit Machchhar managed to regain control of a flydubai aircraft after a co-pilot attacked him. The plane had dropped thousands of feet in a matter of seconds before passengers and crew intervened and the aircraft was eventually diverted to Saudi Arabia. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later identified the captain and praised his actions.

Article Title: Why ‘kaun se wale papa’ remark led to man’s conviction
Article Text:
The court said every rude or offensive remark addressed to a woman would not automatically constitute an offence under Section 509 IPC (AI Image)

“Dekho papa aa gaye, don’t cry.”

“Kaun se wale papa aa gaye?”





NEW DELHI: A Delhi court has convicted a man for insulting a woman’s modesty over a seemingly casual remark, “Kaun se wale papa?”, made when she told her three-year-old daughter that her father had arrived to pick them up from school. Though the two had no prior dispute, the court held that the remark implied the woman had multiple partners and questioned the child’s paternity.Judicial magistrate first class Moksha Bains, in a Sept 24 judgment, said the remark was not an innocuous inquiry about the child’s father but carried an insinuation about the woman’s sexual propriety and fidelity. “The expression, when addressed to a woman in the aforesaid setting, is not an innocuous inquiry as to the identity of a person,” the judge observed, adding that its “obvious insinuation” was that there could be more than one man who could be described as the child’s father.The case dates back to March 23, 2021, when Priyanka Gupta was walking with her three-year-old daughter near RBI Enclave Gate in Paschim Vihar. As the child cried, Gupta told her,Girdhari Lal, who ran a clothes ironing cart at a street corner, then allegedly interjected,Gupta initially ignored the remark and, about two minutes later, handed over the child to her husband after he arrived in a car.She later informed her father-in-law, who called the police, following which an FIR was registered at Paschim Vihar East police station under Section 509 IPC.In his statement under Section 313 CrPC, Lal admitted making the remark but claimed it was not made with any “ill intention”. He also alleged false implication, with the defence arguing that Gupta wanted him removed from the street corner where he had run his ironing business for seven years.Rejecting the defence, the court observed: “The explanation offered by the accused that the words were spoken without ‘ill intention’ is a bare assertion. No surrounding circumstance has been brought on record from which the remark could reasonably acquire an innocent meaning.”The court said every rude or offensive remark addressed to a woman would not automatically constitute an offence under Section 509 IPC, as the insult must have the requisite nexus with her modesty. In this case, however, it held that the remark was personally directed at Gupta and made immediately after she referred to her child’s father, carrying a sexually derogatory insinuation concerning her relationship with men and the child’s paternity.The court held that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and convicted Lal under Section 509 IPC.
Article Summary: A Delhi court has convicted a man for insulting a woman’s modesty over a seemingly casual remark. Priyanka Gupta told her three-year-old daughter that her father had arrived to pick them up from school. Girdhari Lal, who ran a clothes ironing cart at a street corner, then allegedly interjected, “Kaun se wale papa aa gaye?”

Article Title: Hyderabad woman Sandhya Reddy becomes mayor of Sydney council
Article Text:
Sandhya Reddy, originally from Hyderabad, has become the mayor of Strathfield Council in Sydney





HYDERABAD: A Hyderabad-origin woman, Sandhya Reddy, was elected mayor of Strathfield Council in Sydney, Australia, on Tuesday. According to members of the migrant community, she is the first Indian-born migrant woman to serve as a mayor in Australia.Affectionately known as Sandy, Reddy began her journey with the State Emergency Service in 2014 and was elected to the Strathfield Council as an independent councillor in 2021. In 2023, she was elected deputy mayor of the council.A lawyer by profession, Reddy was born and raised in Hyderabad, where she also pursued her education before moving to Australia in 2005. She has been living in the country ever since.Members of the Indian community in Australia hailed her achievement, describing it as both "symbolic and significant" for the country's multicultural communities.
Article Summary: Sandhya Reddy, originally from Hyderabad, has become the mayor of Strathfield Council in Sydney. She is the first Indian-born migrant woman to serve as a mayor in Australia. Reddy began her journey with the State Emergency Service in 2014.

Article Title: Jaipur man held for killing pregnant live-in partner, burying body in rented house courtyard
Article Text:
The murder came to light on Sept 27, (Representative Image)





JAIPUR: Police here Tuesday arrested a 20-year-old man for allegedly strangling his pregnant live-in partner and burying her body in the courtyard of their rented house in Prestige Garden Colony, Bindayaka.DCP (West) Prashant Kiran identified the accused as Pravesh Kumar alias Haggu. Police said he allegedly killed Kiran Rawat on Sept 23 after suspecting her of having an affair with another man. The two were related as nephew and aunt and had been living together as partners.The murder came to light on Sept 27 when the house owner found Kiran’s body buried in the courtyard. Police said Kumar had poured about two kilograms of salt over the body before digging a pit and burying her.During questioning, Kumar told police that he strangled Kiran with one hand and covered her nose and mouth with a cloth with the other. He initially tried to mislead investigators by claiming that Kiran had died by suicide and that he buried her body after panicking, police said.Kumar and Kiran had come to Jaipur from their village about two months ago. Kiran was pregnant and Kumar was living with her and taking care of her.The two used the same mobile phone. Kumar worked odd jobs to support them, police said.After the murder, Kumar allegedly switched off the phone and went to Samod on foot to visit the Hanuman temple.Police said he told them he went there to “wash away his sins”. He returned to work and stayed there from Sept 24 to 26.On Sept 27, after suspecting that the murder had been discovered, Kumar allegedly collected Rs 500 in wages from the factory owner and fled Jaipur.Police teams began searching for him after recovering Kiran’s body. Investigators examined CCTV footage, analysed technical evidence and prepared a route chart to track his movements.A police team eventually detained him on Agra-Lucknow Expressway and arrested him after questioning.Kumar is a resident of Parsa Auliya Lalpur village under Safdarganj police station in Barabanki, Uttar Pradesh.
Article Summary: Pravesh Kumar allegedly killed Kiran Rawat on Sept 23 after suspecting her of having an affair with another man. The two were related as nephew and aunt and had been living together as partners. Police said Kumar had poured about two kilograms of salt over the body before digging a pit and burying her.

Article Title: Blast at MRPL refinery sends loud boom across Mangaluru, thick smoke billows
Article Text:
A loud explosion-like sound was reported from the Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Ltd premises on Wednesday.

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you feel the local authorities managed the situation well after the blast? Yes No 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion





MANGALURU: A blast followed by a fire was reported at the CHT unit, the Hydro Sulphur Treatment Unit of Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Ltd (MRPL), on Wednesday.The fire has since been brought under control, city police commissioner Sudheer Kumar Reddy CH said.One person, identified as Rajesh Baptist, sustained burn injuries covering around 35% of his body and was shifted to Srinivasa Hospital. He is undergoing treatment in the ICU and doctors said he is out of danger.Six other people who suffered minor injuries at an adjacent office were given outpatient treatment and underwent medical check-ups, police said.The city police commissioner, deputy commissioner and Zilla Panchayat CEO are present at the site. Police said there was no major cause for concern and that necessary precautionary measures were being taken.MRPL also confirmed that there were no casualties in the incident and appealed to people not to panic.The blast sent a loud boom across several kilometres, with thick black smoke billowing from the refinery premises. Residents of Jokatte and Surathkal reported that their houses shook and doors and windows vibrated following the explosion.The blast was also reportedly heard at Mangaluru airport, where windows of the administrative office rattled. Fire tenders and emergency teams were rushed to the refinery, while ambulances were seen leaving the premises.On the advice of the district administration, Mangaluru airport is conducting a visual inspection of vital installations in and around the airport, including the Precision Approach Lighting Category I systems and peripheral roads, to check their operational readiness.Dakshina Kannada MP Capt Brijesh Chowta said he was in constant touch with MRPL officials, the police commissioner and Fire and Emergency Services Department officials and was proceeding to the spot to assess the situation.He appealed to people to remain calm, refrain from spreading rumours or misinformation, and cooperate with the administration. Local hospitals were also instructed to remain prepared as a precautionary measure.
Article Summary: A blast followed by a fire was reported at the Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Ltd (MRPL) on Wednesday. One person sustained burn injuries covering around 35% of his body and was shifted to Srinivasa Hospital. Residents of Jokatte and Surathkal reported that their houses shook and doors and windows vibrated.

Article Title: As the US government wants to change the clock 'forever', researchers in Canada warn; call it a 'time bomb' for ...
Article Text:
Why researchers are against 'changing' the clock

Permanent daylight bill: Where it stands right now

A renewed political drive in the United States to end seasonal clock adjustments by locking in year-round Daylight Saving Time is facing resistance from both Capitol Hill and the medical community. While President Donald Trump has put heavy pressure on lawmakers to pass the measure -- calling for extra evening sunshine for recreation and business -- a growing body of scientific evidence warns that the policy could trigger chronic public health damage. Incidentally, some members of Congress in the US have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942. The Senate passed a bill in 2022 to make daylight saving time permanent, but it got stalled in the House.The debate reignited this week with the publication of a research review in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. As several Canadian jurisdictions weigh ending their own clock changes, researchers examined the physiological fallout of permanent daylight saving time compared to permanent standard time.Their findings endorse permanent standard time as the healthier option, cautioning that extended evening light paired with darker winter mornings runs counter to the fundamental biology of the human body. For those unaware, Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the US are set one hour ahead of standard time.According to the authors of the research report, the human circadian rhythm runs on a natural cycle of roughly 24.2 hours and relies critically on natural morning sunlight to reset and synchronize essential bodily functions. While later daylight hours may accommodate evening commutes and outdoor leisure, delayed sunrise suppresses natural wakefulness. Conversely, lingering evening light delays the internal clock, disrupting sleep quality, mood, and daily productivity.The consequences of late-shifted sunlight are already visible along the geographic borders of current time zones, where sunrise and sunset can vary by over an hour within a single zone. The Canadian review cited evidence showing that Americans living on the western edges of time zones -- where the sun sets later -- lose roughly an hour of sleep each week compared to those on the eastern side. The researchers concluded that while abolishing biannual clock adjustments eliminates a few weeks of acute disruption each year, the consequences of permanent daylight saving time would be chronic. Their recommendation aligns with broad consensus across international chronobiology and sleep medicine organizations, including a 2024 guidance from British sleep specialists advocating a permanent lock on Greenwich Mean Time.Called the Sunshine Protection Act, it passed in the House in July this year, but faces roadblocks in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed to it. Proponents, including President Trump and his administration, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Those against, say that permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings.Despite these warnings, legislative momentum in Washington remains contentious. While the U.S. House of Representatives has advanced a measure establishing permanent daylight saving time, the bill has stalled in the Senate. The impasse even prompted President Trump to escalate public pressure, going so far as to post the personal mobile phone number of Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas on social media.Defending his stance, Cotton noted that previous attempts to lock the clock to summer hours collapsed once citizens faced the reality of dark winter mornings. Historical records support the pushback: the United States previously adopted permanent daylight saving time during World War II and again during the 1973 energy crisis, with Congress repealing the 1970s initiative after less than a year amid intense public outcry over morning darkness. Similar nationwide trials in Russia and Chile were also later reversed due to public dissatisfaction, safety concerns, and body-clock disruption.Canadian researchers further note that a permanent shift by the United States would place severe economic pressure on Canada to follow suit, regardless of medical advice.
Article Summary: The U.S. House of Representatives has advanced a measure establishing permanent daylight saving time. The bill has stalled in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed to it. Proponents, including President Trump and his administration, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Those against, say that the policy would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings.

Article Title: Cancer, paralysis leave family fighting on all fronts
Article Text:
Rourkela:





A 57-year-old daily-wage worker from Bargarh district is struggling to keep his family afloat as he juggles the treatment of his cancer-stricken son, paralysed wife and his own heart condition, all amid mounting debt and shrinking income.Netranand Pradhan, a native of Kayatikra village under Janapada panchayat, currently lives with his family at his in-laws’ house in Talipada village of Bargarh district. Employed at a vegetable seed centre, he earns a modest salary that is proving insufficient to meet the family’s spiralling medical expenses.His only son, Balaram Pradhan (21), a first-year degree student who is hearing-impaired and physically challenged, was diagnosed with testicular cancer in May this year. His wife, Laxmi (47), suffered a paralytic stroke three months ago. Netranand himself underwent open-heart surgery in 2024 and requires lifelong medication.After initially taking Balaram to VIMSAR, Burla, the family shifted him to a private hospital in Raipur, where he underwent surgery on May 11. He has since been undergoing regular chemotherapy sessions, requiring frequent trips between Bargarh and Raipur.While chemotherapy expenses are being covered under the Ayushman Bharat scheme, the family spends around Rs 10,000 every month on medicines for Balaram. Netranand said he is also unable to afford a PET-CT scan recommended by doctors.The family’s financial woes have deepened as Laxmi requires hospitalisation and continued treatment for paralysis. According to Netranand, the family is spending nearly Rs 5,000 a month on her medicines and injections. He claimed he has not been able to admit her for further treatment as the family’s health coverage limitations have complicated simultaneous treatment for multiple members.Adding to the burden, Netranand requires medicines worth about Rs 5,000 every month following his heart surgery but often skips treatment because of a lack of money.“I am currently in Raipur for my son’s cancer treatment while my wife is battling paralysis. I earn very little and have no savings. I am borrowing money from relatives and acquaintances to buy medicines for my son and wife. Even I am unable to buy all the medicines prescribed for me. Life has become extremely painful,” he said.With medical expenses mounting and debts rising, the family is now relying on borrowed money and goodwill support to continue treatment for all three members. .
Article Summary: Netranand Pradhan, 57, lives with his family at his in-laws’ house in Talipada village of Bargarh district. His only son, Balaram, 21, was diagnosed with testicular cancer in May this year. His wife, Laxmi (47), suffered a paralytic stroke three months ago. Netranand himself underwent open heart surgery in 2024 and requires lifelong medication.

Article Title: 105 Children ‘Adopted’ Under Single Samagra ID: Five Booked in Madhya Pradesh
Article Text: Bhopal: An administrative inquiry in Damoh has uncovered what appears to be a major manipulation of Samagra records, with 105 children found registered under a single family ID, multiple children shown as “Adopted” and records allegedly shifted between different families using forged or questionable documents. The findings, spanning alleged irregularities over more than 11 years from January 2013 to June 2024, have now resulted in an FIR against six people at Damoh Dehat police station. Officials are trying to search and locate these children and their current status, say sources.The case followed a complaint by Damoh district Bal Kalyan Samiti chairperson Deepak Tiwari, who approached the district collector with allegations concerning irregular registration of children and manipulation of their records. The collector ordered a four-member inquiry, which examined the Samagra records and supporting documents before the FIR was registered.Officials are now probing whether the alleged manipulation was merely a case of fraudulent data entries or whether the records point to a larger network involving the identity and placement of children besides religious conversion.Investigations zeroed in on Samagra family ID 40777745, under which the inquiry found 105 children/members registered at different points of time.Several children were recorded as “Adopted” in relation to the family head. The inquiry examined the documents submitted for their registration and allegedly found discrepancies in the supporting records. It concluded that registrations based on such documents were contrary to the prescribed procedure.The inquiry also found instances in which children’s records were allegedly transferred from one family ID to another. In one case, a child whose Samagra ID was recorded as 132503068 was initially registered under family ID 42304379, headed by Sanjeev Lewart.The inquiry found that the child’s record was subsequently transferred through the Janpad Panchayat Damoh login and added to family ID 40777745, the same ID carrying records of 105 children. The entry was later deleted, according to the FIR.The inquiry held Dilip, a Janpad Panchayat employee, responsible in connection with registration based on allegedly forged documents and also held Lewart responsible for getting the child added to his family without following the prescribed procedure.The inquiry found similar entries in other family IDs. In family ID 25395117, headed by Praveen Paul, a child was recorded with the relationship “Adopted”. The inquiry questioned the documents used for the registration. In another case, family ID 43507123, headed by Ramlal Kashyap, had three children recorded as “Adopted”.The inquiry examined the identity and birth date and Aadhaar-related records of the children. In one of the cases, it reportedly found discrepancies between the person reflected in the family records and the person appearing in other records.A religious conversion angle is under probe. Tiwari said, “I had raised the matter with the district collector, who got the matter inquired into and got the FIR registered. The circumstances surrounding these registrations warrant a deeper probe, including the possibility of a religious-conversion angle, so that the facts and the larger chain behind them can be established.”Investigators are trying to establish whether there is any connection between the alleged manipulation of children’s identities, the “adopted” entries and any religious-conversion activity. The FIR names Sanjeev Lewart, Ramlal Kashyap, Praveen Paul, Jagdish, Parth Rajpoot and Dilip under various sections.
Article Summary: Investigations zeroed in on Samagra family ID 40777745, under which the inquiry found 105 children/members registered at different points of time. Several children were recorded as “Adopted” in relation to the family head. A religious conversion angle is under probe.

Article Title: 3 years after October 7 Hamas attack: A scarred Israel, a devastated Gaza and a Middle East no longer the same
Article Text:
Israelis mark the October 7 anniversary in Israel as Gaza continues to bear the war’s devastating toll

Benny and Maggy Solomon, parents of Oct 7 victim Hila Solomon, attend a memorial at the Nova festival site in southern Israel (Credit: AP)

October 7, 2023: Day the ‘iron’ wall broke

A minute-by-minute look at how the October 7 assault broke through Israel’s border defences.

Palestinian children walk amid the rubble of buildings destroyed during Gaza war (Credit: Reuters)

Gaza became war's price, and its unfinished question

Even after years of war, the biggest questions over Gaza’s governance, security, disarmament and rebuilding remain open

The war crossed the fence, then crossed borders

Iran's ‘axis of resistance’ stopped looking invincible

The conflict widened from Gaza to Lebanon, the Red Sea, Iraq, Syria and eventually direct Israel-Iran confrontation

Shadow war finally came into open

Israel won battlefield. What does it do with power?

Palestinians at centre, increasingly without control

Gulf states no longer just watching from sidelines

Three years of war have reshaped the balance of power across the Middle East

3 years on, Oct 7 is still reshaping map

From Gaza’s ruins to a global shock

Three years after Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the shockwaves of that day continue to shape lives, politics and security across the Middle East. What began as a devastating assault on southern Israel grew into a prolonged war in Gaza and then widened into a regional confrontation involving Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran and Iran-backed groups.The conflict has left behind two deeply traumatic realities - the Israeli experience of the attack, hostage-taking and continuing security fears, and the Palestinian devastation caused by the war in Gaza. Beyond the immediate human cost, the conflict has also altered alliances, weakened Iran’s regional network, changed Israel’s military calculations and disrupted diplomatic efforts across the region.For those who lived through October 7, however, the consequences are not measured only in geopolitical shifts. They remain embedded in ordinary moments, places and memories, reminders of a day that transformed the meaning of safety, freedom and home.“The smell of hell.”That is how one Israeli resident describes what a barbecue now smells like.Living close to Gaza, Deganit Bar Hay told AP the smell of burnt flesh has become a trigger, making it difficult for her to barbecue.Along the highway running parallel to the Gaza Strip, where people were gunned down while trying to flee on October 7, memorials now stand beside the road.Cars smashed and riddled with bullets have been preserved elsewhere, stacked in rusting heaps. Portraits of young female military spotters, whose warnings about a possible attack were disregarded, mark another set of lives lost that day.For those who survived the attack and those who were taken hostage, the meaning of ordinary life changed too.“Freedom has completely changed the way I see life,” Emily Damari, who was abducted wounded from her home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza and released in January 2025, told Reuters.After captivity, she said, even opening a refrigerator or drinking cold water felt like something to be grateful for. “Being free, at home, surrounded by my family and my people is something I will never take for granted again.”Eli Sharabi, taken hostage from nearby Kibbutz Be'eri, spent 491 days in captivity. His wife Lianne and daughters Noiya and Yahel were killed in the October 7 attack, while his brother Yossi was taken hostage and died in Gaza. Released in February 2025 emaciated after what he said was prolonged hunger, shackling and beatings, Sharabi told Reuters: “I choose life. I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do. ”Three years later, those memories remain raw in Israel. But there is another landscape of memory just across the border.In Gaza, children are growing up with different reminders of the same war - lost parents, amputations, displacement, damaged homes and years without anything resembling a normal childhood. DW reported the stories of 15-year-old Mahmoud Abu Shadaq, recovering from injuries caused by an airstrike, and eight-year-old Layan Abed, who lost her father during the conflict.Aid groups are providing rehabilitation and mental-health support, but the scars are likely to outlast the fighting.That is the paradox at the heart of the three years since October 7.One attack produced two vastly different but deeply traumatic legacies - the Israeli trauma of the assault and hostage-taking, and the Palestinian devastation that followed Israel's military campaign in Gaza.And the consequences did not stop at Gaza's borders.What began with Hamas's assault on southern Israel became a war in Gaza, then a wider confrontation involving Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran and Iran-backed groups across the region. It has altered Israel's security doctrine, weakened Iran's regional network, unsettled Arab states, disrupted diplomacy and pushed the Middle East into a new and still uncertain balance of power.Three years on, the question is no longer simply what happened on October 7. It is what October 7 set in motion.Just before 6.30am on October 7, 2023, Israel’s much-vaunted “iron wall” along Gaza began to fail. Explosives dropped by drones knocked out communication towers and remote-controlled guns, while snipers targeted sensors and cameras. Israeli defenders were left staring at blank screens as roughly 2,200 rockets rained towards southern and central Israel.Then came the breach. Hamas fighters cut through the 20-foot-high fence or blew openings into it. Motorbikes, pickup trucks and bulldozers poured through, followed by hundreds of armed men. Others arrived on motorised paragliders. About 30 breaches were eventually made, allowing an estimated 1,500 fighters into Israel, The Guardian reported.It was more than a fence being breached. It was the collapse of an assumption — that Israel’s technology, intelligence and military superiority had made a large-scale assault from Gaza almost impossible.“We have decided to put an end to all of the occupation’s crimes,” Hamas commander Mohammed Deif announced as the attack began, declaring the “al-Aqsa deluge”.Within hours, the assault had turned deadly. Fighters stormed military positions and nearby communities, reaching the Supernova music festival, where at least 260 people were killed and others taken hostage. In kibbutzim such as Be’eri, residents barricaded themselves inside reinforced rooms as gunmen moved through the communities. At Zikim, soldiers at a military base were overwhelmed before reinforcements arrived.Files, images, and data analysis are unavailable until usage resets tomorrow at 2:01 AM. Continue chatting with text only, or upgrade for more access.The scale of the failure soon became clear.Israeli intelligence had detected increased communications activity among militants in Gaza before the attack. Egyptian security services had also warned of an impending event. But Israeli officials assessed the activity as connected to a military exercise and decided that the alert level did not need to be raised, The Guardian reported. Three surveillance balloons used to monitor the border had also broken down and had not been replaced.The result was a catastrophic intelligence and preparedness failure: a border designed to keep Gaza's militants out became a route into Israel, while the forces meant to respond were caught unprepared.For people inside the communities along the border, the technological failure quickly became intensely personal.In Nirim, resident Eldad Hess and his family hid inside a reinforced shelter as gunfire erupted outside. “Ten minutes later we heard automatic rifle shots outside the house,” Hess told The Guardian. “I understood what was happening but in my heart I couldn't believe what was happening.”His family survived. Others did not.By late morning, Israel had declared war. At 10.34am, Israeli strikes began hitting Gaza. At 11.35am, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Israelis: “Citizens of Israel, we are at war. Not an operation, not a round – at war.”The language of the conflict changed almost as quickly as its geography.The attack had begun as a meticulously planned assault on southern Israel. Within hours, it had become the opening act of a war that would transform Gaza, redraw Israel's security calculations and eventually pull much of the Middle East into its orbit.The military campaign that followed October 7 devastated Gaza.Entire neighbourhoods were destroyed, millions were displaced and a generation of children has grown up amid death, injury and uncertainty. The humanitarian crisis became one of the defining consequences of the war.Even after a ceasefire agreement in October 2025 secured the release of the remaining hostages and hundreds of Palestinian prisoners and detainees, the larger Gaza question remained unresolved.According to Reuters, Israeli strikes have continued despite the ceasefire. Gaza's health ministry says at least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the truce, while Israel says its strikes target Hamas and accuses the group of trying to rearm and carry out attacks. Hamas denies the accusation.Meanwhile, Israel's effective control over Gaza has expanded to around two-thirds of the enclave, Reuters reported. The advance of the Israeli-controlled “yellow line” has squeezed Gaza's roughly 2 million residents into a shrinking coastal area where many live in tents or damaged buildings.The numbers tell one part of the story. The more difficult question is what happens next.Trump's plan envisaged Hamas disarming, Israeli forces gradually withdrawing, an International Stabilization Force taking over security and a new Palestinian technocratic administration governing Gaza.None of those pieces has fully fallen into place.The proposed force has a commander and commitments from several countries but has yet to be assembled. A Palestinian technocratic governing body appointed in January has yet to enter Gaza. Hamas has indicated a willingness to hand its weapons over for storage under a US-backed Palestinian administration, but Israel has rejected any withdrawal before complete disarmament.And reconstruction is barely beginning.A $2.45 billion plan announced by the Board of Peace in September is dwarfed by an EU-UN estimate of $71.4 billion needed for recovery and reconstruction over the next decade, Reuters reported.The war may have ended in parts of Gaza. The question of what Gaza becomes has not.The first major regional spillover came from Lebanon.Hezbollah, Iran's most powerful regional ally, entered the conflict, opening another front along Israel's northern border. What had been a long-running Israel-Hezbollah confrontation now became part of the October 7 war.Then came Yemen.The Houthis attacked Israel and targeted shipping in the Red Sea, turning a conflict thousands of kilometres away into a threat to one of the world's busiest maritime corridors. US and British military action followed.Iran-backed groups in Iraq and Syria also became part of the wider confrontation.The significance was larger than the individual attacks. October 7 demonstrated that a war involving Israel and Hamas could activate an entire network of armed groups built over decades.And then the network itself began to fracture.Before October 7, Iran's regional influence appeared formidable.Hamas governed Gaza. Hezbollah possessed a vast arsenal in Lebanon. Bashar al-Assad remained in power in Syria. The Houthis controlled large parts of Yemen and threatened shipping lanes. Behind them stood Iran, whose missiles and nuclear programme had long been central to Israeli and Western security calculations.Three years later, that picture has been transformed.Hamas lost its top leadership, including Yahya Sinwar, who was killed by Israel in October 2024. Hezbollah suffered major losses. Assad is no longer in power in Syria. Iran's own territory has come under direct Israeli and US military attack.“The old order — Iran as the region's disruptive spine, its proxies as the tools of pressure and deterrence — is gone,” Bilal Saab, a Chatham House fellow and former Pentagon official, told The Washington Post.Ali Vaez, director of the Iran Project at the International Crisis Group, put the change more starkly: “This has changed the region forever.”But a weakened Iran does not automatically mean a more stable Middle East.For decades, Israel and Iran largely fought without declaring a conventional war against each other — through proxies, covert operations, assassinations, cyberattacks and strikes on Iranian-linked targets.October 7 accelerated the collapse of that distance.The confrontation increasingly moved from the shadows into direct exchanges of missiles and drones, exposing the limits of the old system of indirect deterrence.For Israel, the result has been a dramatic increase in military dominance.A former senior Israeli military official told The Washington Post that, despite the continuing trauma of October 7 and the ongoing war, Israel had reached a position few had imagined possible.“We are still traumatized from 7th October. There is still war,” the official said. “Israel is not untouchable, but we have made it very expensive to touch us.”That may be Israel's biggest strategic transformation since the attack: October 7 produced not only a determination to prevent another such assault, but a willingness to use overwhelming force far beyond its immediate borders.Military dominance brings its own dilemma.Israel's neighbours may have welcomed the weakening of Iran and its allies, but the emergence of an Israel with fewer regional constraints has also created unease.“The focus on security comforts Israelis but unnerves their neighbors,” The Washington Post reported, citing regional analysts. An Israel less constrained by powerful rivals raises questions about whether military superiority could turn into overreach, particularly in the West Bank.Saab told the paper that Gulf leaders, while wanting to see the Iranian regime weakened, also worry about “the trigger-happiness of Israel”.Inside Israel, however, the emerging philosophy is increasingly being framed as security through strength.“When this is over, I think you're going hear our leaders talk about Israel's desire for peace through strength,” an Israeli official told The Washington Post. “We are going to fight our enemies as strongly as possible and hug our friends as close as possible.”The shift is significant.For much of its history, Israel's military strength was primarily presented as a shield. After October 7, the war has pushed Israel towards using that strength to actively reshape the strategic environment around it.Whether that creates lasting security remains one of the region's biggest unanswered questions.There is another paradox.The war has put the Palestinian question back at the centre of international diplomacy. Yet Palestinians themselves have little control over what comes next.Gaza has been devastated and its population repeatedly displaced. The future of its governance remains unsettled. In the West Bank, settlement expansion and calls for Palestinian displacement have intensified.The debate over Gaza's future has also exposed sharply different visions.Trump's plan says Gaza should be rebuilt for its people. Israeli right-wing politicians have called for “voluntary emigration”. Israel's defence ministry established an office in 2025 to oversee such departures after Trump had suggested Gazans could be permanently displaced. Trump later backed away from the idea following strong opposition from Arab states and international criticism.The competing visions leave Gaza caught between reconstruction, Israeli security demands, Hamas's future and the unresolved question of Palestinian statehood.The October 7 attack was intended by Hamas to alter the regional balance. Instead, Palestinians have emerged from the war facing a destroyed territory and an uncertain political future.The war has also changed the calculations of countries that were not direct combatants.Saudi Arabia had been moving towards a potentially transformative relationship with Israel before October 7. The war disrupted that trajectory and pushed the Palestinian question back into the centre of Arab diplomacy.At the same time, Gulf states have had to watch Iran's missiles and drones reach closer to their own territory.Saudi Arabia and Turkey are emerging as important players in the next regional order. Both are deepening relationships with China, maintaining channels with Russia and continuing to work with Washington — a form of strategic hedging as they assess what a more powerful Israel and a less predictable US presence mean for them.The Gulf's old calculation was relatively straightforward: American security guarantees, economic stability and the containment of regional rivalries.After October 7, none of those assumptions looks quite as secure.The most consequential change may be that the region no longer has the same centre of gravity.Before October 7, Iran's network of armed allies was at the height of its influence. Israel was powerful but largely operated within a familiar system of deterrence. Arab states were cautiously pursuing normalisation and economic integration. The Palestinian issue, while unresolved, had increasingly been pushed into the background of regional diplomacy.The attack shattered that equilibrium.Israel emerged more militarily dominant but also more isolated. Gaza emerged devastated. Iran's regional network was badly weakened, but the collapse of that network created uncertainty rather than a settled alternative. Saudi Arabia and Turkey gained greater room to manoeuvre. Gulf states became more conscious of their own vulnerability. The US remained indispensable but its regional choices became more consequential — and more controversial.The result is not necessarily a new Middle East yet.It is a Middle East in transition.“This has changed the region forever,” Vaez told The Washington Post. “But with what consequences still has to play out.”And perhaps that is the clearest measure of what three years of war have changed.For an Israeli survivor, the smell of a barbecue can still bring October 7 back.For a child in Gaza, an airstrike can mean a missing parent, an injured body or another lost home.For Iran, Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and the Gulf states, the same three years have rewritten calculations about power and security.The attack began with a breach in a border fence.Three years later, the breach has become a fault line running through the entire Middle East.The deepest consequences of October 7 are still visible in Gaza, where three years of war have transformed everyday life. Homes, neighbourhoods and essential infrastructure have been devastated, while repeated displacement has uprooted much of the territory’s roughly two million people.The destruction has extended far beyond buildings. Gaza’s economy has been pushed into collapse, with 92% of economic establishments damaged or destroyed and unemployment reaching 78%, according to UN figures cited in September. Nearly 98% of schools have been damaged or destroyed, while Gaza’s health system has been left barely functioning. For many families, access to water, electricity, shelter, healthcare and education has become a daily struggle.The war has also reshaped the geography of Gaza. Israeli military control and restrictions have pushed Palestinians into increasingly smaller areas, while the so-called Yellow Line has become a new dividing point inside the territory. The result is a population living amid destroyed homes, damaged infrastructure and limited access to basic services, even after the October 2025 ceasefire.But the economic consequences did not remain confined to Gaza or the Middle East.The war disrupted energy markets and global supply chains, with the Strait of Hormuz emerging as a critical pressure point. Around 25-30% of global oil and about 20% of liquefied natural gas pass through the waterway, exposing major energy importers in Asia and Europe to higher fuel and power costs.Shipping disruptions have increased freight and insurance costs, while interruptions to fertiliser supplies have raised concerns over food prices. The shock is particularly severe for poorer countries, where food accounts for a larger share of household spending and governments have less fiscal space to absorb higher costs.Financial markets have also felt the effects, with higher borrowing costs, tighter financial conditions and increased volatility adding to pressures on economies already carrying heavy debt burdens.The IMF has described the shock as global but uneven: energy importers are more exposed than exporters, poorer countries more than richer ones, and economies with limited reserves more than those with stronger buffers.That may be the widest legacy of October 7. The attack began in southern Israel, but its consequences have travelled through Gaza's ruins, across the region's borders and into the world's energy, food, trade and financial systems.Three years on, October 7 is no longer only a date that changed the Middle East. It has become a fault line whose economic and geopolitical aftershocks continue to reach far beyond it.
Article Summary: Three years after Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the shockwaves of that day continue to shape lives, politics and security across the Middle East. What began as a devastating assault on southern Israel grew into a prolonged war in Gaza and then widened into a regional confrontation involving Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iran and Iran-backed groups.

Article Title: In 2016, an Arkansas woman put one wooden pantry outside a church with food and toiletries; within three months the idea had gone global, and the movement now maps 2,301 mini pantries
Article Text:
The idea soon travelled beyond Fayetteville and Arkansas, developing into networks of mini pantries in communities across the United States and elsewhere. Some local networks began maintaining their own maps, including the Lowcountry Blessing Box Project and Pātaka Kai Open Street Pantries.

From books to basic needs

A community takes ownership

A small idea spreads

The power of something small

Sometimes an idea for helping people does not begin with a foundation, a fundraiser or a grand plan. Sometimes it starts with a small wooden box, a few cans of food and the simple realisation that a neighbourhood can look after its own. In Fayetteville, Arkansas, Jessica McClard was fascinated by the Little Free Library movement, which was bringing tiny book-sharing structures into neighbourhoods. She began wondering whether the same principle could be applied to something more immediate than books. What if people could share food, toiletries and everyday essentials in exactly the same way?In May 2016, that question became the Little Free Pantry and that slowly became a huge success. Scroll down to read this success story.According to ABC News, McClard installed what she believed to be the first Little Free Pantry outside Good Shepherd Lutheran Church in Fayetteville. The small wooden structure was stocked with canned food, personal-care products, paper goods and other necessities. The model was deliberately uncomplicated. People who had something to spare could leave it. Anyone who needed something could take it.There were no forms, membership cards or complicated systems to navigate.The pantry quickly demonstrated how much demand existed for such a simple resource. Items that disappeared particularly quickly included deodorant, toothpaste, toothbrushes, diapers, feminine hygiene products, toilet paper and paper towels. Food remained important, but the experiment also highlighted how expensive everyday necessities can become when household budgets are stretched.What made the pantry distinctive was not simply what was placed inside it, but what happened around it. As per the same report, people began adding school supplies for children and other useful items. The structure itself became something of a community canvas, with neighbours decorating it for occasions such as Memorial Day. The pantry was no longer just McClard's project. It had begun to belong to the neighbourhood. Handwritten thank-you notes left inside the pantry became another small but meaningful sign of its impact. The reach also extended beyond the immediate area, with people travelling from other places to visit the original pantry.The idea soon travelled beyond Fayetteville and Arkansas, developing into networks of mini pantries in communities across the United States and elsewhere. Some local networks began maintaining their own maps, including the Lowcountry Blessing Box Project and Pātaka Kai Open Street Pantries, adds the official website of Little Free Pantry. The wider movement now maps 2,301 mini pantries, illustrating how a hyper-local experiment can develop into a much broader community-driven network, the website adds.The project has also found connections with wider cultural and charitable initiatives. In 2021, the Little Free Pantry partnered with Celadon Books and the Jane Goodall Institute around the launch of Jane Goodall's The Book of Hope, bringing the idea of everyday community action into a broader conversation about hope and collective responsibility.The lasting appeal of the Little Free Pantry lies partly in its simplicity. It does not attempt to solve food insecurity through a sweeping programme. Instead, it creates a visible point where one person can help another without ceremony. Its success also reveals something easily overlooked about community support: people do not always need to be told how to help. Sometimes they simply need a place to put their generosity.Image Courtesy: The Chronicle of Philanthropy
Article Summary: Jessica McClard installed the first Little Free Pantry outside a church in Fayetteville, Arkansas, in May 2016. The small wooden structure was stocked with canned food, personal-care products, paper goods and other necessities. The model was deliberately uncomplicated. People who had something to spare could leave it.

Article Title: ‘Protesters are students, not anti-social elements’: Bombay HC on MPSC stir
Article Text:
The Bombay HC affirmed students' right to protest against suspected wrongdoing in the MPSC exams

HC says protesting students have right to agitate

HC asks students to return to studies

Bombay HC seeks roadmap from Maharashtra govt





MUMBAI: The Bombay high court on Wednesday said students protesting against alleged malpractices in Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC) examinations were “not anti-social elements” and stressed that the state government must ensure recruitment exams are conducted fairly and without irregularities.The court also said aggrieved students have the right to protest, while urging them to return to their studies as it examined their grievances.A bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna said the government must assure students that examinations would be conducted in an “impartial, fair” manner and without malpractices.The court was hearing a petition filed by Pune residents against the ongoing agitation in the city by students and others over alleged malpractices in MPSC examinations and other examination-related controversies.The bench said the government must make sincere efforts to restore the confidence of people, particularly students, in the examination system."If they (students) do not have an opportunity and they get the idea that there has been hanky panky, they have the right to agitate. Because they have given hours of study," the court said.Advocate General Milind Sathe, appearing for the state government, said authorities had shown reasonable restraint and had not registered any FIRs against the protesters.He also said most of the demands raised by the agitators had been met."One of their demands was the resignation of the MPSC Chairman. A recommendation has been sent to the Governor as per the procedure and further action is awaited," Sathe said.Appreciating the government's decision not to lodge cases against the protesters, the court said, "The protesters are students. They are not anti-social elements."The court, however, urged the students to return to their education as the matter was now before the court."The court is now seized of the matter and the trust should be restored. Their grievances should be addressed. Free and fair examinations should take place. I will look into how the state is moving. They should trust the court," the HC said.It also asked the protesters to consider the difficulties faced by their families and return to their colleges."These children are innocent, but now they are on the roads. Their careers will be spoilt," Chief Justice Tripathi said, while also asking the protesters to ensure that no hardship was caused to the peace-loving city and its residents.The bench directed the state government to submit a roadmap and a report within three weeks.The matter has been posted for further hearing on November 25.The petition, filed by Pune residents Amit Supekar and Sourabh Virkar, named the state government as well as protest organisers Pramod Patil, Nitin Andhale and Chetan Wagaj as respondents.One of the organisers told the court that they would withdraw their agitation, while the other two said they were willing to relocate their protest to any place provided by the Pune authorities.(With PTI inputs)
Article Summary: Bombay HC affirms students' right to protest against suspected wrongdoing in the MPSC exams. Court says protesting students have right to agitate but urges them to return to studies. Court asks state government to submit a roadmap and a report within three weeks.

Article Title: ‘Fight won’t be easy’: CJP warns of prolonged agitation ahead of Oct 10 protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar
Article Text:
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convenor and spokesperson Saurav Das at a press conference ahead of Jantar Mantar protest





NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and student organisations on Wednesday called for a united mobilisation against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar ahead of their October 10 protest, saying the agitation would continue until the electoral system was overhauled.At a joint press conference, the groups sought to put their campaign against the Election Commission (EC) on a broader political footing, backing the opposition INDIA bloc MPs' October 6 protest march and describing the confrontation as one between people defending democracy and the BJP.In July, a CJP-led agitation over the NEET paper leak had forced Dharmendra Pradhan to resign as Union education minister, news agency PTI reported.The group is now seeking to sustain street pressure against Kumar as protests against the EC intensify ahead of October 10.Wednesday's press conference brought together the CJP, All India Students' Association (AISA), All India Students' Federation (AISF) and Students' Federation of India (SFI).The Aam Aadmi Party 's student wing, Association of Students for Alternative Politics (ASAP), also participated.CJP co-convener Saurav Das urged people across the country to travel to Delhi and be prepared for a prolonged agitation, PTI reported."This fight is not going to be easy. I appeal to everyone across the country to join us, book train and flight tickets," he said.Das said protesters would not back down even if Kumar resigned, as the electoral system needed cleaning up. He alleged that the BJP's pushback reflected a "lust for eternal power".The demands outlined by Das include Kumar's resignation and initiation of criminal proceedings against him; freezing the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls; halting upcoming elections; restoring the January 2025 voters' list and ordering an independent inquiry; and repealing the 2023 law governing appointments to the EC to establish an independent and credible selection process.AISA president Neha Bora said there was no division between the student-led mobilisation and the opposition parties' protests.She said common people, civil society, opposition parties and student organisations stood on one side and the EC and the BJP on the other, PTI reported."There are no divisions. We, the people of India, versus the BJP. If we lead this fight unitedly, we will do it effectively," Bora said.Backing the INDIA bloc MPs who tried to march towards the EC office on Tuesday demanding Kumar's resignation, she said elected representatives had a duty to take to the streets to raise people's issues and defend their rights."That's what the MPs of the INDIA bloc did," she said, adding that the CJP and student organisations of opposition parties would lend strength to the October 10 protest."If ever there was a time to desert the BJP, it is now," Bora said, urging those in the BJP camp to join people seeking to defend democracy and the Constitution.The projection of unity comes days after online sparring between the CJP and sections aligned with the Congress.Das said the participants were united regardless of political affiliations and ideologies in a larger fight to change a "broken system", PTI reported.Asked whether the organisers would obtain permission for the protest, Das said they had submitted a formal intimation at the Parliament Street police station on Wednesday and provided undertakings."Please don't use the word permission. Who is Delhi Police to give us permission?" he said, adding that intimation was sufficient."We will cooperate with Delhi Police and we hope Delhi Police will cooperate with us," he added.SFI's Adarsh Shaji accused Kumar of undermining Indian democracy, describing the confrontation as a fight between "democracy and autocracy".(With agency inputs)
Article Summary: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and student organisations call for a united mobilisation against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The groups sought to put their campaign against the Election Commission (EC) on a broader political footing. The group is now seeking to sustain street pressure against Kumar as protests against the EC intensify ahead of October 10.

Article Title: ‘Not reflected on Google Maps’: Delhi Police flags heavy congestion on Barapulla Phase-III; commuters to take alternate routes
Article Text:
Delhi Traffic Police issued an advisory due to heavy congestion on Barapulla Phase-III Elevated Road

Why is Barapulla facing congestion?





NEW DELHI: Delhi Traffic Police on Wednesday issued an advisory after heavy congestion was reported on Barapulla Phase-III Elevated Road towards Barapulla and Ring Road from Noida Link Road and Mayur Vihar Phase-I.In a post on X, Delhi Traffic Police said, "Congestion on Barapulla Phase-III is not being reflected on Google Maps, due to which commuters are continuing to use this route. This has resulted in heavy traffic and a bottleneck at Barapulla Junction".Traffic towards Barapulla and Ring Road was heavy and slow-moving. To ease the congestion, traffic from Barapulla Phase-III was being diverted towards NH-24/DND.Commuters were advised to avoid the affected stretch and take alternate routes via NH-24/DND, while traffic personnel were deployed at the spot to regulate movement.Earlier, Delhi Traffic Police said traffic from around eight to nine lanes was converging into just three lanes at a single point on the older flyover stretch.The traffic police said the Old Barapullah Flyover has three lanes, while the newly opened Phase-III flyover on the Mayur Vihar side, the Sarai Kale Khan loop and the DND loop each have around three lanes. The convergence of these roadways creates the bottleneck.The clarification came after a journalist posted about a 2-km traffic jam from Mayur Vihar towards AIIMS, claiming that even an ambulance had been caught in the congestion.The traffic snarls emerged soon after the opening of Barapulla Phase-III, which was expected to improve connectivity between Mayur Vihar and Sarai Kale Khan and ease movement towards central Delhi.
Article Summary: Heavy congestion reported on Barapulla Phase-III Elevated Road. Commuters advised to avoid stretch and take alternate routes via NH-24/DND. Delhi Traffic Police said traffic from around eight to nine lanes was converging into just three lanes at a single point.
